prompt: How many processing units are 3 Spanner nodes?
Which of these instance sizes does Spanner refuse?
hint: Steps of 100 below 1,000, whole nodes above.

choices.text: 100 processing units, a tenth of a node
choices.why: The smallest instance Spanner sells, a tenth of a node.

choices.text: 900 processing units
choices.why: A multiple of 100 below 1,000.

choices.text: 1,500 processing units
choices.why: Right. Above 1,000 the steps are whole nodes, 1,000 at a time.

choices.text: 5 nodes, which is 5,000 processing units
choices.why: 5,000 processing units, a whole number of nodes.

prompt: Where do a Spanner database's compute capacity and replica placement come from?

choices.text: Each table declares its own
choices.why: Tables are declared by the schema and share the database's instance.

choices.text: The instance it lives in
choices.why: Right. Databases inside one instance share its capacity and configuration.

choices.text: The database, chosen when it is created
choices.why: `databases create` takes a schema, not a size or a placement.

choices.text: The project's default region
choices.why: The configuration is chosen per instance, with `--config`.

prompt: Why is a key that counts up, 1, 2, 3, a problem in Spanner and not in a single-server PostgreSQL?
hint: Where does the next row go, and who serves that place?

choices.text: Spanner cannot index integers
choices.why: Integer keys are fine; their order is the problem.

choices.text: All new rows land in the last range
choices.why: Right. The table's write rate becomes one server's.

choices.text: Counters run out faster in Spanner
choices.why: INT64 is the same size everywhere.

choices.text: Spanner hashes integer keys, so neighbours separate
choices.why: Spanner keeps rows sorted by key; it does not hash them.

prompt: In the lesson's run, why did `BySequence` put exactly 50 new rows in each quarter while `ByUuid` did not?
hint: One is random and one is constructed.

choices.text: The emulator rounds the counts
choices.why: The counts are what the program counted.

choices.text: UUIDs are longer than integers, so they sort into fewer places
choices.why: Length does not decide where a key sorts.

choices.text: Bit-reversal spreads consecutive numbers evenly
choices.why: Right. A UUID version 4 is random, so its spread varies a little per run.

choices.text: The sequence was reset between the two tables
choices.why: Both tables were filled once; the sequence was not reset.

prompt: Quitanda logs app clicks into a Spanner table keyed by `(ClickTime, ClickId)`. Writes stall at one server's rate. Which change helps most?
hint: What does the first column of the key decide?

choices.text: Add nodes to the instance
choices.why: More nodes do not help if every write lands in one key range.

choices.text: Make `ClickId` a UUID and keep `ClickTime` first
choices.why: The first column still counts up, so new rows still go to the end.

choices.text: Put `UserId` first in the key
choices.why: Right. Writes from many users spread over many ranges, and one user's clicks stay in order.

choices.text: Interleave the table in `Customers`
choices.why: Interleaving needs the parent's key first, and would not fix time order on its own.

prompt: Spanner cuts a table into contiguous ranges of keys, each served by one server at a time. One such range is a ___.
hint: The lesson's figure draws four of them.

prompt: What does `INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Customers` do to `Orders`?

choices.text: Copies each order into the customer's row
choices.why: Rows stay separate; they are stored next to each other.

choices.text: Stores the orders next to their customer
choices.why: Right. A customer and their orders are one contiguous run of keys.

choices.text: Creates a foreign key and nothing else
choices.why: It enforces the parent, and its purpose is where the rows are stored.

choices.text: Hashes the orders across all servers
choices.why: It does the opposite: it keeps one customer's orders together.

prompt: Why was `OrderNotes`, keyed by `(OrderId)`, refused as a child of `Customers`?
hint: Read what the error asked for.

choices.text: Its key does not begin with `CustomerId`
choices.why: Right. The child's key has to start with the parent's for the placement to exist.

choices.text: A table cannot be interleaved in a table that already has a child
choices.why: A parent may have several interleaved children.

choices.text: `STRING(MAX)` columns cannot be interleaved
choices.why: Column types are not the problem; the key is.

choices.text: Notes should be interleaved in `Stock`
choices.why: Notes belong to orders; the error was about the key.

prompt: Quitanda's accountants want deleting a customer to fail while the customer has orders. What should the schema say?
hint: Cascade is one of two choices.

choices.text: `ON DELETE CASCADE`
choices.why: That deletes the orders with the customer, which is what they do not want.

choices.text: `ON DELETE NO ACTION`
choices.why: Right. The delete of a parent is refused while it has children.

choices.text: Nothing; Spanner never deletes a parent with children
choices.why: With `ON DELETE CASCADE`, as in the lesson, it deletes them all.

choices.text: A stale read before every delete
choices.why: A read does not stop a delete; the schema does.

prompt: `order.py c-99 banana 1 690` was refused. What happened to the stock `UPDATE` that had already run inside the transaction?

choices.text: It was committed, and the stock is one banana short
choices.why: The stock still read 6 afterwards.

choices.text: It was rolled back
choices.why: Right. It went with the refused `INSERT`. Nothing in a transaction becomes visible unless all of it commits.

choices.text: It was retried until the customer existed
choices.why: A refused write is not retried; an aborted transaction is.

choices.text: It was kept as a stale version, readable in the past
choices.why: An uncommitted write never existed at any timestamp.

prompt: Which Quitanda read is a good place for a stale read of 15 seconds?

choices.text: The checkout taking the last bananas
choices.why: It acts on the number, so it reads strongly, inside its transaction.

choices.text: The catalogue's stock count
choices.why: Right. A number a few seconds old is good enough, and any up-to-date replica can answer.

choices.text: A refund that checks the order was paid
choices.why: Money decisions read the latest committed state.

choices.text: The order confirmation shown after the commit
choices.why: It must show the write that just happened, which only a strong read guarantees.

prompt: `run_in_transaction` may run your function more than once. Which version of `place` would be a bug?

choices.text: One that reads the stock inside the function
choices.why: That is `order.py`, and each retry reads afresh.

choices.text: One that raises `ValueError` when stock is short
choices.why: Raising rolls back and is not retried.

choices.text: One reusing a count read before the transaction
choices.why: Right. A retry would reuse a value that may no longer be true.

choices.text: One that writes the order with `THEN RETURN`
choices.why: Returning the key is safe on every attempt.

prompt: In `two.py`, the rice update committed on its third attempt, seconds late. What does that tell you about Spanner?

choices.text: Spanner locks the whole table during a transaction
choices.why: Spanner locks rows; the rows here were different.

choices.text: Nothing; it is the emulator's limit
choices.why: Right. The emulator runs one read-write transaction at a time; Spanner would have committed both at once.

choices.text: Transactions on different rows conflict in Spanner
choices.why: They do not; that is the emulator's limit.

choices.text: The client library is misconfigured
choices.why: Its retries are what eventually committed the rice.

prompt: At 1.35 USD per node-hour, what does a Standard instance of 300 processing units cost for 730 hours?
Quitanda wants its Spanner database to keep writing if all of São Paulo is lost. Which edition does the pricing page say that needs?

choices.text: Standard
choices.why: Standard is a regional instance.

choices.text: Enterprise
choices.why: Enterprise adds read-only replicas, not dual- or multi-region configurations.

choices.text: Enterprise Plus
choices.why: Right. Dual-region and multi-region configurations are Enterprise Plus.

choices.text: Any edition, with `--config=emulator-config`
choices.why: That configuration exists only in the emulator.

prompt: An emulator instance was created with `--edition=ENTERPRISE` and the São Paulo configuration, and both were accepted. What can you conclude about a real project?

choices.text: The project may use that configuration and edition
choices.why: The emulator checks neither; it accepted a configuration not in its own list.

choices.text: Nothing; the emulator recorded no edition and checked no configuration
choices.why: Right. Those two have to be checked against Google Cloud itself.

choices.text: Enterprise is the default edition
choices.why: The description showed no edition at all.

choices.text: The instance would cost 134.69 a month
choices.why: The arithmetic is right for Enterprise, but the emulator proved nothing about it.

choices.text: A read-write transaction rolled back as a whole

choices.text: Where a hotspot makes one server busy
